entries.dfbd725e39b41683fa9ce4c8923f3cd70b931fe9: <div sID="gen17777" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="26" osisID="Jer.26" sID="Jer.26"/> <div eID="gen17777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17778" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17779" type="x-p"/> As in the history of the Acts of the Apostles that of their preaching and that of their suffering are interwoven, so it is in the account we have of the prophet Jeremiah; witness this chapter, where we are told, I. How faithfully he preached, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. How spitefully he was persecuted for so doing by the priests and the prophets, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.7-Jer.26.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. III. How bravely he stood to his doctrine, in the face of his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.12-Jer.26.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. IV. How wonderfully he was protected and delivered by the prudence of the princes and elders, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.16-Jer.26.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. Though Urijah, another prophet, was about the same time put to death by Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.23">ver. 20-23</reference>), yet Jeremiah met with those that sheltered him, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">ver. 24</reference>.
entries.b42012933db1915d8633261c302b2230acaebc70: <div eID="gen17779" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17778" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Solemn Address. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17780" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah came this word from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Stand in the court of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, and speak unto all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word: <hi type="super">3</hi> If so be they will hearken, and turn every man from his evil way, that I may repent me of the evil, which I purpose to do unto them because of the evil of their doings. <hi type="super">4</hi> And thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; If ye will not hearken to me, to walk in my law, which I have set before you, <hi type="super">5</hi> To hearken to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent unto you, both rising up early, and sending <hi type="italic">them,</hi> but ye have not hearkened; <hi type="super">6</hi> Then will I make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth. <div eID="gen17780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17781" type="x-p"/> We have here the sermon that Jeremiah preached, which gave such offence that he was in danger of losing his life for it. It is here left upon record, as it were, by way of appeal to the judgment of impartial men in all ages, whether Jeremiah was worthy to die for delivering such a message as this from God, and whether his persecutors were not very wicked and unreasonable men. <div eID="gen17781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17782" type="x-p"/> I. God directed him where to preach this sermon, and when, and to what auditory, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.2">v. 2</reference>. Let not any censure Jeremiah as indiscreet in the choice of place and time, nor say that he might have delivered his message more privately, in a corner, among his friends that he could confide in, and that he deserved to smart for not acting more cautiously; for God gave him orders to preach <hi type="italic">in the court of the Lord's house,</hi> which was within the peculiar jurisdiction of his sworn enemies the priests, and who would therefore take themselves to be in a particular manner affronted. He must preach this, as it should seem, at the time of one of the most solemn festivals, when persons had come from all the <hi type="italic">cities of Judah</hi> to <hi type="italic">worship in the Lord's house.</hi> These worshippers, we may suppose, had a great veneration for their priests, would credit the character they gave of men, and be exasperated against those whom they defamed, and would, consequently, side with them and strengthen their hands against Jeremiah. But none of these things must move him or daunt him; in the face of all this danger he must preach this sermon, which, if it were not convincing, would be very provoking. And because the prophet might be in some temptation to palliate the matter, and make it better to his hearers than God had made it to him, to exchange an offensive expression for one more plausible, therefore God charges him particularly <hi type="italic">not to diminish a word,</hi> but to speak all the things, nay, <hi type="italic">all the words,</hi> that he had commanded him. Note, God's ambassadors must keep closely to their instructions, and not in the least vary from them, either to please men or to save themselves from harm. They must neither <hi type="italic">add</hi> nor <hi type="italic">diminish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">Deut. iv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen17782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17783" type="x-p"/> II. God directed him what to preach, and it is that which could not give offence to any but such as were resolved to go on still in their trespasses. 1. He must assure them that if they would <hi type="italic">repent of their sins,</hi> and turn from them, though they were in imminent danger of ruin and desolating judgments were just at the door, yet a stop should be put to them, and God would proceed no further in his controversy with them, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.3">v. 3</reference>. This was the main thing God intended in sending him to them, to try if they would return from their sins, that so God might turn from his anger and turn away the judgments that threatened them, which he was not only willing, but very desirous to do, as soon as he could do it without prejudice to the honour of his justice and holiness. See how God <hi type="italic">waits to be gracious,</hi> waits till we are duly qualified, till we are fit for him to be gracious to, and in the mean time tries a variety of methods to bring us to be so. 2. He must, on the other hand, assure them that if they continued obstinate to all the calls God gave them, and would persist in their disobedience, it would certainly end in the ruin of their city and temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.4-Jer.26.6">v. 4-6</reference>. (1.) That which God required of them was that they should be observant of what he had said to them, both by the written word and by his ministers, that they should <hi type="italic">walk in all his law which he set before them,</hi> the law of Moses and the ordinances and commandments of it, and that they should <hi type="italic">hearken to the words of his servants the prophets,</hi> who pressed nothing upon them but what was agreeable to the law of Moses, which was <hi type="italic">set before them</hi> as a touchstone to try the spirits by; and by this they were distinguished from the false prophets, who drew them from the law, instead of drawing them to it. The law was what God himself set before them. The prophets were his own servants, and were immediately sent by him to them, and sent with a great deal of care and concern, <hi type="italic">rising early to send them,</hi> lest they should come too late, when their prejudices had got possession and become invincible. They had hitherto been deaf both to the law and to the prophets: <hi type="italic">You have not hearkened.</hi> All he expects now is that at length they should heed what he said, and make his word their rule—a reasonable demand. (2.) That which is threatened in case of refusal is that this city, and the temple in it, shall fare as their predecessors did, Shiloh and the tabernacle there, for a like refusal to walk in God's law and hearken to his prophets, then when the present dispensation of prophecy just began in Samuel. Now could a sentence be expressed more unexceptionably? Is it not a rule of justice <hi type="italic">ut parium par sit ratio—that those whose cases are the same be dealt with alike?</hi> If Jerusalem be like Shiloh in respect of sin, why should it not be like Shiloh in respect of punishment? Can any other be expected? This was not the first time he had given them warning to this effect; see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12-Jer.7.14">ch. vii. 12-14</reference>. When the temple, which was the glory of Jerusalem, was destroyed, the city was thereby <hi type="italic">made a curse;</hi> for the temple was that which made it a blessing. <hi type="italic">If the salt lose</hi> that <hi type="italic">savour, it is thenceforth good for nothing.</hi> It shall be <hi type="italic">a curse,</hi> that is, it shall be the pattern of a curse; if a man would curse any city, he would say, <hi type="italic">God make it like Jerusalem!</hi> Note, Those that will not be subject to the commands of God make themselves subject to the curse of God.
entries.4433f0a31205abef6af3c2b481bf1f58d894f4af: <div eID="gen17783" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah Prosecuted for His Preaching; Jeremiah's Defence. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17784" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> So the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> Now it came to pass, when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had commanded <hi type="italic">him</hi> to speak unto all the people, that the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die. <hi type="super">9</hi> Why hast thou prophesied in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">10</hi> When the princes of Judah heard these things, then they came up from the king's house unto the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and sat down in the entry of the new gate of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's <hi type="italic">house.</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> Then spake the priests and the prophets unto the princes and to all the people, saying, This man <hi type="italic">is</hi> worthy to die; for he hath prophesied against this city, as ye have heard with your ears. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then spake Jeremiah unto all the princes and to all the people, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that ye have heard. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you. <hi type="super">14</hi> As for me, behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you. <hi type="super">15</hi> But know ye for certain, that if ye put me to death, ye shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves, and upon this city, and upon the inhabitants thereof: for of a truth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sent me unto you to speak all these words in your ears. <div eID="gen17784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17785" type="x-p"/> One would have hoped that such a sermon as that in the <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.6">foregoing verses</reference>, so plain and practical, so rational and pathetic, and delivered in God's name, would work upon even this people, especially meeting them now at their devotions, and would prevail with them to repent and reform; but, instead of awakening their convictions, it did but exasperate their corruptions, as appears by this account of the effect of it. <div eID="gen17785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17786" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah is charged with it as a crime that he had preached such a sermon, and is apprehended for it as a criminal. The <hi type="italic">priests,</hi> and <hi type="italic">false prophets,</hi> and <hi type="italic">people, heard him speak these words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.7">v. 7</reference>. They had patience, it seems, to hear him out, did not disturb him when he was preaching, nor give him any interruption till he had <hi type="italic">made an end of speaking all that the Lord commanded him to speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.8">v. 8</reference>. So far they dealt more fairly with him than some of the persecutors of God's ministers have done; they let him say all he had to say, and yet perhaps with a bad design, in hopes to have something worse yet to lay to his charge; but, having no worse, this shall suffice to ground an indictment upon: He hath said, <hi type="italic">This house shall be like Shiloh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.9">v. 9</reference>. See how unfair they are in representing his words. He had said, in God's name, <hi type="italic">If you will not hearken to me, then will I make this house like Shiloh;</hi> but they leave out God's hand in the desolation (<hi type="italic">I will make</hi> it so) and their own hand in it in not hearkening to the voice of God, and charge it upon him that he <hi type="italic">blasphemed this holy place,</hi> the crime charged both on our Lord Jesus and on Stephen: He said, <hi type="italic">This house shall be like Shiloh.</hi> Well might he complain, as David does (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.5">Ps. lvi. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Every day they wrest my words;</hi> and we must not think it strange if we, and what we say and do, be thus misrepresented. When the accusation was so weakly grounded, no marvel that the sentence passed upon it was unjust: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt surely die.</hi> What he had said agreed with what God had said when he took possession of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.6-1Kgs.9.8">1 Kings ix. 6-8</reference>), <hi type="italic">If you shall at all turn from following after me, then this house shall be</hi> abandoned; and yet he is condemned to die for saying it. It is not out of any concern for the honour of the temple that they appear thus warm, but because they are resolved not to part with their sins, in which they flatter themselves with a conceit that the <hi type="italic">temple of the Lord</hi> will protect them; therefore, right or wrong, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt surely die.</hi> This outcry of the priests and prophets raised the mob, and <hi type="italic">all the people were gathered together against Jeremiah</hi> in a popular tumult, ready to pull him to pieces, were <hi type="italic">gathered about him</hi> (so some read it); they flocked together, some crying one thing and some another. <hi type="italic">The people</hi> that were at first present were hot against him (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.8">v. 8</reference>), but their clamours drew more together, only to see what the matter was. <div eID="gen17786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17787" type="x-p"/> II. He is arraigned and indicted for it before the highest court of judicature they had. Here, 1. The <hi type="italic">princes of Judah</hi> were his judges, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.10">v. 10</reference>. Those that filled the thrones of judgment, <hi type="italic">the thrones of the house of David,</hi> the elders of Israel, they, hearing of this tumult in the temple, <hi type="italic">came up from the king's house,</hi> where they usually sat near the court, <hi type="italic">to the house of the Lord,</hi> to enquire into this matter, and to see that nothing was done disorderly. They <hi type="italic">sat down in the entry of the new gate of the Lord's house,</hi> and held a court, as it were, by a special commission of <hi type="italic">Oyer and Terminer.</hi> 2. The <hi type="italic">priests and prophets</hi> were his prosecutors and accusers, and were violently set against him. They appealed to <hi type="italic">the princes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to all the people,</hi> to the court and the jury, whether <hi type="italic">this man</hi> were not <hi type="italic">worthy to die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">v. 11</reference>. The corrupt priests and counterfeit prophets have always been the most bitter enemies of the prophets of the Lord; they had ends of their own to serve, which they thought such preaching as this would be an obstruction to. When Jeremiah prophesied in the house of the king concerning the fall of the royal family (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.1">ch. xxii. 1</reference>, &c.), the court, though very corrupt, bore it patiently, and we do not find that they persecuted him for it; but when he comes into the <hi type="italic">house of the Lord,</hi> and touches the copyhold of the priests, and contradicts the lies and flatteries of the false prophets, then he is adjudged <hi type="italic">worthy to die.</hi> For the prophets <hi type="italic">prophesied falsely,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">priests bore rule by their means,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">ch. v. 31</reference>. Observe, When Jeremiah is indicted before the princes the stress of his accusation is laid upon what he said concerning the city, because they thought the princes would be most concerned about that. But concerning the words spoken they appeal to the people, "<hi type="italic">You have heard</hi> what he hath said; let it be given in evidence." <div eID="gen17787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17788" type="x-p"/> III. Jeremiah makes his defence before the princes and the people. He does not go about to deny the words, nor to diminish aught from them; what he has said he will stand to, though it cost him his life; he owns that he had prophesied against <hi type="italic">this house</hi> and <hi type="italic">this city,</hi> but, 1. He asserts that he did this by good authority, not maliciously nor seditiously, not out of any ill-will to his country nor any disaffection to the government in church or state, but, <hi type="italic">The Lord sent me</hi> to prophesy thus: so he begins his apology (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.12">v. 12</reference>), and so he concludes it, for this is that which he resolves to abide by as sufficient to bear him out (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Of a truth the Lord hath sent me unto you, to speak all these words.</hi> As long as ministers keep closely to the instructions they have from heaven they need not fear the opposition they may meet with from hell or earth. He pleads that he is but a messenger, and, if he faithfully deliver his message, he must bear no blame; but he is a messenger from the Lord, to whom they were accountable as well as he, and therefore might demand regard. If he speak but what God appointed him to speak, he is under the divine protection, and whatever affront they offer to the ambassador will be resented by the Prince that sent him. 2. He shows them that he did it with a good design, and that it was their fault if they did not make a good use of it. It was said, not by way of fatal sentence, but of fair warning; if they would take the warning, they might prevent the execution of the sentence, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.13">v. 13</reference>. Shall I take it ill of a man that tells me of my danger, while I have an opportunity of avoiding it, and not rather return him thanks for it, as the greatest kindness he could do me? "<hi type="italic">I have</hi> indeed (says Jeremiah) prophesied <hi type="italic">against this city;</hi> but, <hi type="italic">if you will now amend your ways and your doings,</hi> the threatened ruin shall be prevented, which was the thing I aimed at in giving you the warning." Those are very unjust who complain of ministers for preaching hell and damnation, when it is only to keep them from that place of torment and to bring them to heaven and salvation. 3. He therefore warns them of their danger if they proceed against him (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for me,</hi> the matter is not great what become of me; <hi type="italic">behold, I am in your hand;</hi> you know I am; I neither have any power, nor can make any interest, to oppose you, nor is it so much my concern to save my own life: <hi type="italic">do with me as seems meet unto you;</hi> if I be led to the slaughter, it shall be as a lamb." Note, It becomes God's ministers, that are warm in preaching, to be calm in suffering and to behave submissively to the powers that are over them, though they be persecuting powers. But, for themselves, he tells them that it is at their peril if they put him to death: <hi type="italic">You shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.15">v. 15</reference>. They might think that killing the prophet would help to defeat the prophecy, but they would prove wretchedly deceived; it would but add to their guilt and aggravate their ruin. Their own consciences could not but tell them that, if Jeremiah was (as certainly he was) sent of God to bring them this message, it was at their utmost peril if they treated him for it as a malefactor. Those that persecute God's ministers hurt not them so much as themselves.
entries.4949dc6cfee69dc594d48f39e6b3d0a4cfd91242: <div eID="gen17788" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Acquittal; Jeremiah's Deliverance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen17789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Then said the princes and all the people unto the priests and to the prophets; This man <hi type="italic">is</hi> not worthy to die: for he hath spoken to us in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then rose up certain of the elders of the land, and spake to all the assembly of the people, saying, <hi type="super">18</hi> Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and spake to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Zion shall be plowed <hi type="italic">like</hi> a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest. <hi type="super">19</hi> Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and besought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls. <hi type="super">20</hi> And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim, who prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: <hi type="super">21</hi> And when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death: but when Urijah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt; <hi type="super">22</hi> And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> Elnathan the son of Achbor, and <hi type="italic">certain</hi> men with him into Egypt. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people. <hi type="super">24</hi> Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death. <div eID="gen17789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17790" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The acquitting of Jeremiah from the charge exhibited against him. He had indeed spoken the words as they were laid in the indictment, but they are not looked upon to be seditious or treasonable, ill-intended or of any bad tendency, and therefore the court and country agree to find him not guilty. The priests and prophets, notwithstanding his rational plea for himself, continued to demand judgment against him; but the princes, and all the people, are clear in it that <hi type="italic">this man is not worthy to die</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.16">v. 16</reference>); for (say they) <hi type="italic">he hath spoken to us,</hi> not of himself, but <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord our God.</hi> And are they willing to own that he did indeed speak to them <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord</hi> and that that Lord is their God? Why then did they not amend their ways and doings, and take the method he prescribed to prevent the ruin of their country? If they say, His prophecy is <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> it may justly be asked, <hi type="italic">Why did you not then believe him?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.25">Matt. xxi. 25</reference>. Note, It is a pity that those who are so far convinced of the divine original of gospel preaching as to protect it from the malice of others do not submit to the power and influence of it themselves. <div eID="gen17790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17791" type="x-p"/> II. A precedent quoted to justify them in acquitting Jeremiah. Some of the <hi type="italic">elders of the land,</hi> either the princes before mentioned or the more intelligent men of the people, stood up, and put the assembly in mind of a former case, as is usual with us in giving judgment; for the wisdom of our predecessors is a direction to us. The case referred to is that of Micah. We have extant the book of his prophecy among the minor prophets. 1. Was it thought strange that Jeremiah prophesied against this city and the temple? Micah did so before him, even in the reign of Hezekiah, that reign of reformation, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">v. 18</reference>. Micah said it as publicly as Jeremiah had now spoken to the same purport, <hi type="italic">Zion shall be ploughed like a field,</hi> the building shall be all destroyed, so that nothing shall hinder but it may be ploughed; <hi type="italic">Jerusalem shall become heaps</hi> of ruins, and <hi type="italic">the mountain of the house</hi> on which the temple is built shall be <hi type="italic">as the high places of the forest,</hi> overrun with briers and thorns. That prophet not only spoke this, but wrote it, and left it on record; we find it, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>. By this it appears that a man may be, as Micah was, a true prophet of the Lord, and yet may prophesy the destruction of Zion and Jerusalem. When we threaten secure sinners with the taking away of the Spirit of God and the kingdom of God from them, and declining churches with the removal of the candlestick, we say no more than what has been said many a time, and what we have warrant from the word of God to say. 2. Was it thought fit by the princes to justify Jeremiah in what he had done? It was what Hezekiah did before them in a like case. Did Hezekiah, and the people of Judah (that is, the representatives of the people, the commons in parliament), did they complain of Micah the prophet? Did they impeach him, or make an act to silence him and put him to death? No; on the contrary, they took the warning he gave them. Hezekiah, that renowned prince, of blessed memory, set a good example before his successors, for he <hi type="italic">feared the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.19">v. 19</reference>), as Noah, who, being <hi type="italic">warned of God of things not seen as yet,</hi> was <hi type="italic">moved with fear.</hi> Micah's preaching drove him to his knees; he <hi type="italic">besought the Lord</hi> to turn away the judgment threatened and to be reconciled to them, and he found it was not in vain to do so, for <hi type="italic">the Lord repented him of the evil</hi> and returned in mercy to them; he sent an angel, who routed the army of the Assyrians, that threatened to plough <hi type="italic">Zion like a field.</hi> Hezekiah got good by the preaching, and then you may be sure he would do no harm to the preacher. These elders conclude that it would be of dangerous consequence to the state if they should gratify the importunity of the priests and prophets in putting Jeremiah to death: <hi type="italic">Thus might we procure great evil against our souls.</hi> Note, It is good to deter ourselves from sin with the consideration of the mischief we shall certainly do to ourselves by it and the irreparable damage it will be to our own souls. <div eID="gen17791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17792" type="x-p"/> III. Here is an instance of another prophet that was put to death by Jehoiakim for prophesying as Jeremiah had done, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20">v. 20</reference>, &c. Some make this to be urged by the prosecutors, as a case that favoured the prosecution, a modern case, in which speaking such words as Jeremiah had spoken was adjudged treason. Others think that the elders, who were advocates for Jeremiah, alleged this to show that thus they might <hi type="italic">procure great evil against their souls,</hi> for it would be adding sin to sin. Jehoiakim, the present king, had slain one prophet already; let them not fill up the measure by slaying another. Hezekiah, who protected Micah, prospered; but did Jehoiakim prosper who slew Urijah? No; they all saw the contrary. As good examples, and the good consequences of them, should encourage us in that which is good, so the examples of bad men, and the bad consequences of them, should deter us from that which is evil. But some good interpreters take this narrative from the historian that penned the book, Jeremiah himself, or Baruch, who, to make Jeremiah's deliverance by means of the princes the more wonderful, takes notice of this that happened about the same time; for both were in the reign of Jehoiakim, and this <hi type="italic">in the beginning of his reign,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, 1. Urijah's prophecy. It was <hi type="italic">against this city, and this land, according to all the words of Jeremiah.</hi> The prophets of the Lord agreed in their testimony, and one would have thought that out of the mouth of so many witnesses the word would be regarded. 2. The prosecution of him for it, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.21">v. 21</reference>. Jehoiakim and his courtiers were exasperated against him, and <hi type="italic">sought to put him to death;</hi> in this wicked design the king himself was principally concerned. 3. His absconding thereupon: <hi type="italic">When he heard</hi> that the king had become his enemy, and sought his life, <hi type="italic">he was afraid, and fled, and went in to Egypt.</hi> This was certainly his fault, and an effect of the weakness of his faith, and it sped accordingly. He distrusted God, and his power to protect him and bear him out; he was too much under the power of that <hi type="italic">fear of man</hi> which <hi type="italic">brings a snare.</hi> It looked as if he durst not stand to what he had said or was ashamed of his Master. It was especially unbecoming him to flee <hi type="italic">into Egypt,</hi> and so in effect to abandon the land of Israel and to throw himself quite out of the way of being useful. Note, There are many that have much grace, but they have little courage, that are very honest, but withal very timorous. 4. His execution notwithstanding. Jehoiakim's malice, one would think, might have contented itself with his banishment, and it might suffice to have driven him out of the country; but those are <hi type="italic">bloodthirsty</hi> that <hi type="italic">hate the upright,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Prov. xxix. 10</reference>. It was the life, that precious life, that he hunted after, and nothing else would satisfy him. So implacable is his revenge that he sends a party of soldiers into Egypt, some hundreds of miles, and they bring him back by force of arms. It would not sufficiently gratify him to have him slain in Egypt, but he must feed his eyes with the bloody spectacle. They <hi type="italic">brought him to Jehoiakim,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">slew him with the sword,</hi> for aught I know with his own hands. Yet neither did this satisfy his insatiable malice, but he loads the dead body of the good man with infamy, would not allow it the decent respects usually and justly paid to the remains of men of distinction, but cast it into <hi type="italic">the graves of the common people,</hi> as if he had not been a prophet of the Lord; thus was the <hi type="italic">shield of Saul vilely cast away, as though he had not been anointed with oil.</hi> Thus Jehoiakim hoped both to ruin his reputation with the people, that no heed might be given to his predictions, and to deter others from prophesying in like manner; but in vain; Jeremiah says the same. There is no contending with the word of God. Herod thought he had gained his point when he had cut off John Baptist's head, but found himself deceived when, soon after, he heard of Jesus Christ, and said, in a fright, <hi type="italic">This is John the Baptist.</hi> <div eID="gen17792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17793" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is Jeremiah's deliverance. Though Urijah was lately put to death, and persecutors, when they have tasted the blood of saints, are apt to thirst after more (as Herod, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.2-Acts.12.3">Acts xii. 2, 3</reference>), yet God wonderfully preserved Jeremiah, though he did not flee, as Urijah did, but stood his ground. Ordinary ministers may use ordinary means, provided they be lawful ones, for their own preservation; but those that had an extraordinary protection. God raised up a friend for Jeremiah, whose hand was with him; he took him by the hand in a friendly way, encouraged him, assisted him, appeared for him. It was <hi type="italic">Ahikam the son of Shaphan,</hi> one that was a minister of state in Josiah's time; we read of him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.12">2 Kings xxii. 12</reference>. Some think Gedaliah was the son of this Ahikam. He had a great interest, it should seem, among the princes, and he used it in favour of Jeremiah, to prevent the further designs of the priests and prophets against him, who would have had him turned over <hi type="italic">into the hand of the people,</hi> not those people (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.16">v. 16</reference>) that had adjudged him innocent, but the rude and insolent mob, whom they could persuade by their cursed insinuations not only to cry, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">stone him to death</hi> in a popular tumult; for perhaps Jehoiakim had been so reproached by his own conscience for slaying Urijah that they despaired of making him the tool of their malice. Note, God can, when he pleases, raise up great men to patronize good men; and it is an encouragement to us to trust him in the way of duty that he has all men's hearts in his hands.  <chapter eID="Jer.26"/> <div eID="gen17793" type="x-p"/>

entries.1152be02af6c7a388a145cc5b69983701fcebde1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10153"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.24">Jr 26:1-24</reference>. Jeremiah Declared Worthy of Death, but by the Interposition of Ahikam Saved; the Similar Cases of Micah and Urijah Being Adduced in the Prophet's Favor.</title> <div sID="gen18110" type="x-p"/> The prophecies which gave the offense were those given in detail in the seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.26.6">Jr 26:6</reference> here with <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jr 7:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.14">14</reference>); and summarily referred to here [Maurer], probably pronounced at one of the great feasts (that of tabernacles, according to Ussher; for the inhabitants of "all the cities of Judah" are represented as present, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.2">Jr 26:2</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.1">Jr 7:1</reference>.<div eID="gen18110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10153"/><hi type="bold">2. in the court--</hi>the largest court, from which he could be heard by the whole people.<div eID="gen18111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to worship--</hi>Worship is vain without obedience (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.21">1Sa 15:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen18112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the words--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.10">Eze 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen18113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diminish not a word--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">De 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.32">12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.6">Pr 30:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Ac 20:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.19">Re 22:19</reference>). Not suppressing or softening aught for fear of giving offense; nor setting forth coldly and indirectly what can only by forcible statement do good. <div eID="gen18114" type="x-p"/>
entries.62cc91c372d295944df5760cc6a2880526eb80a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10154"/><div sID="gen18115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10154"/><hi type="bold">3. if so be--</hi>expressed according to human conceptions; not as if God did not foreknow all contingencies, but to mark the obstinacy of the people and the difficulty of healing them; and to show His own goodness in making the offer which left them without excuse [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18115" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc5e685ebc6903bb86d0b49988992af5885c92bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10155"/><div sID="gen18116" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10155"/><hi type="bold">5. prophets--</hi>the inspired interpreters of the law (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.4">Jr 26:4</reference>), who adapted it to the use of the people. <div eID="gen18116" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4658c333a0670f60397a5390934343c36b8f38e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10156"/><div sID="gen18117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10156"/><hi type="bold">6. like Shiloh--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jr 7:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.10-1Sam.4.12">1Sa 4:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference>).<div eID="gen18117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curse--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jr 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.15">Is 65:15</reference>). <div eID="gen18118" type="x-p"/>
entries.c24c252f12a02afa74ef347496c25651672409df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10157"/><div sID="gen18119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10157"/><hi type="bold">8. priests--</hi>The captain (or prefect) of the temple had the power of apprehending offenders in the temple with the sanction of the priests.<div eID="gen18119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophets--</hi>the false prophets. The charge against Jeremiah was that of uttering falsehood in Jehovah's name, an act punishable with death (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">De 18:20</reference>). His prophecy against the temple and city (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">Jr 26:11</reference>) might speciously be represented as contradicting God's own words (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>). Compare the similar charge against Stephen (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.13">Ac 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen18120" type="x-p"/>
entries.37526fe3b66f96c81dcaeb794ac700e2a2e7d063: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10158"/><div sID="gen18121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10158"/><hi type="bold">10. princes--</hi>members of the Council of State or Great Council, which took cognizance of such offenses.<div eID="gen18121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard--</hi>the clamor of the popular tumult.<div eID="gen18122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came up--</hi>from the king's house to the temple, which stood higher than the palace.<div eID="gen18123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat--</hi>as judges, in the gate, the usual place of trying such cases.<div eID="gen18124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new gate--</hi>originally built by Jotham ("the higher gate," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.35">2Ki 15:35</reference>) and now recently restored. <div eID="gen18125" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e39c9de977c4d9ae15716cb3a19b2d495296577: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10159"/><div sID="gen18126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10159"/><hi type="bold">12. Lord sent me--</hi>a valid justification against any laws alleged against him.<div eID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against ... against--</hi>rather, "concerning." Jeremiah purposely avoids saying, "against," which would needlessly irritate. They had used the same Hebrew word (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.11">Jr 26:11</reference>), which ought to be translated "concerning," though they meant it in the unfavorable sense. Jeremiah takes up their word in a better sense, implying that there is still room for repentance: that his prophecies aim at the real good of the city; for or concerning this house ... city [Grotius]. <div eID="gen18127" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb69c3a9e4a8a0128048f3a4ddd8f2eefd41bcf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10160"/><div sID="gen18128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10160"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.3">Jr 26:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.19">19</reference>). <div eID="gen18128" type="x-p"/>
entries.54de9f66a6d1c1eb63ebb949155e596e92897e87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10161"/><div sID="gen18129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10161"/>14. Jeremiah's humility is herein shown, and submission to the powers that be (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Ro 13:1</reference>). <div eID="gen18129" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad981fd49038f76b895bbec0b17ea6c99114029b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10162"/><div sID="gen18130" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10162"/><hi type="bold">15. bring ... upon yourselves--</hi>So far will you be from escaping the predicted evils by shedding my blood, that you will, by that very act, only incur heavier penalties (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Mt 23:35</reference>). <div eID="gen18130" type="x-p"/>
entries.53cdc9bc1a07d18a24259084e5384593b23e3ddd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10163"/><div sID="gen18131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10163"/><hi type="bold">16. princes ... all the people--</hi>The fickle people, as they were previously influenced by the priests to clamor for his death (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.8">Jr 26:8</reference>), so now under the princes' influence require that he shall not be put to death. Compare as to Jesus, Jeremiah's antitype, the hosannas of the multitude a few days before the same people, persuaded by the priests as in this case, cried, Away with Him, crucify Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.11.27">Mt 21:1-11; 27</reference>:20-25). The priests, through envy of his holy zeal, were more his enemies than the princes, whose office was more secular than religious. A prophet could not legally be put to death unless he prophesied in the name of other gods (therefore, they say, "in the name of the Lord"), or after his prophecy had failed in its accomplishment. Meanwhile, if he foretold calamity, he might be imprisoned. Compare Micaiah's case (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.28">1Ki 22:1-28</reference>). <div eID="gen18131" type="x-p"/>
entries.479c301aad5b0f2f0a809d4c7c9a85e70442b3df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10164"/><div sID="gen18132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10164"/>17. Compare Gamaliel's interposition (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.34">Ac 5:34</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen18132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elders--</hi>some of the "princes" mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.16">Jr 26:16</reference>) those whose age, as well as dignity, would give weight to the precedents of past times which they adduce. <div eID="gen18133" type="x-p"/>
entries.947d9b82c25ea6a8e19544827f8e2433840b6529: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10165"/><div sID="gen18134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10165"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Morasthite--</hi>called so from a village of the tribe Judah.<div eID="gen18135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hezekiah--</hi>The precedent in the reign of such a good king proved that Jeremiah was not the only prophet, or the first, who threatened the city and the temple without incurring death.<div eID="gen18136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountain of the house--</hi>Moriah, on which stood the temple (peculiarly called "the house") shall be covered with woods instead of buildings. Jeremiah, in quoting previous prophecies, never does so without alteration; he adapts the language to his own style, showing thereby his authority in his treatment of Scripture, as being himself inspired. <div eID="gen18137" type="x-p"/>
entries.3eebbe6b57dfb875ebe1172b5e685d0064dc9acf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10166"/><div sID="gen18138" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10166"/>19. Hezekiah, so far from killing him, was led "to fear the Lord," and pray for remission of the sentence against Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.26">2Ch 32:26</reference>).<div eID="gen18138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord repented--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.32.14">Ex 32:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.16">2Sa 24:16</reference>).<div eID="gen18139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thus--</hi>if we kill Jeremiah. <div eID="gen18140" type="x-p"/>
entries.59ef7b635146a6c295caed1630197ddf3f87a692: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10167"/><div sID="gen18141" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10167"/>20. As the flight and capture of Urijah must have occupied some time, "the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim" (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.1">Jr 26:1</reference>) must not mean the very beginning, but the second or third year of his eleven years' reign.<div eID="gen18141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And ... also--</hi>perhaps connected with <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jr 26:24</reference>, as the comment of the writer, not the continuation of the speech of the elders: "And although also a man that prophesied ... Urijah ... (proving how great was the danger in which Jeremiah stood, and how wonderful the providence of God in preserving him), nevertheless the hand of Ahikam," &c. [Glassius]. The context, however, implies rather that the words are the continuation of the previous speech of the elders. They adduce another instance besides that of Micah, though of a different kind, namely, that of Urijah: he suffered for his prophecies, but they imply, though they do not venture to express it, that thereby sin has been added to sin, and that it has done no good to Jehoiakim, for that the notorious condition of the state at this time shows that a heavier vengeance is impending if they persevere in such acts of violence [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18142" type="x-p"/>
entries.606cb9f1cc96506cccf6354ad74d218c1dbe4b2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10168"/><div sID="gen18143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10168"/><hi type="bold">22. Jehoiakim sent ... into Egypt--</hi>He had been put on the throne by Pharaoh of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:34</reference>). This explains the readiness with which he got the Egyptians to give up Urijah to him, when that prophet had sought an asylum in Egypt. Urijah was faithful in delivering his message, but faulty in leaving his work, so God permitted him to lose his life, while Jeremiah was protected in danger. The path of duty is often the path of safety. <div eID="gen18143" type="x-p"/>
entries.90e914be99798b7f82a0ab3aea87d3eb1d70039f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10169"/><div sID="gen18144" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10169"/><hi type="bold">23. graves of the common people--</hi>literally, "sons of the people" (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">2Ki 23:6</reference>). The prophets seem to have had a separate cemetery (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.29">Mt 23:29</reference>). Urijah's corpse was denied this honor, in order that he should not be regarded as a true prophet. <div eID="gen18144" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd30737140f5a1ed9f1ef0f33616980568c4a70b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10170"/><div sID="gen18145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10170"/><hi type="bold">24. Ahikam--</hi>son of Shaphan the scribe, or royal secretary. He was one of those whom King Josiah, when struck by the words of the book of the law, sent to inquire of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.12">2Ki 22:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.14">14</reference>). Hence his interference here in behalf of Jeremiah is what we should expect from his past association with that good king. His son, Gedaliah, followed in his father's steps, so that he was chosen by the Babylonians as the one to whom they committed Jeremiah for safety after taking Jerusalem, and on whose loyalty they could depend in setting him over the remnant of the people in Judea (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.14">Jr 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.22">2Ki 25:22</reference>).<div eID="gen18145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people to put him to death--</hi>Princes often, when they want to destroy a good man, prefer it to be done by a popular tumult rather than by their own order, so as to reap the fruit of the crime without odium to themselves (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.20">Mt 27:20</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.26"/>

entries.031f72b7d55aed15f58b88bb85f68cd57d1db336: <div eID="gen29988" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29991" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah, by the commend of God, goes into the court of the Lord's house; and foretells the destruction of the temple and city, if not prevented by the speedy repentance of the people, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.7">Jer 26:1-7</reference>. By this unwelcome prophecy his life was in great danger; although saved by the influence of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, who makes a masterly defense for the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.8-Jer.26.18">Jer 26:8-18</reference>. Urijah is condemned, but escapes to Egypt; whence he is brought hack by Jehoiakim, and slain, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.23">Jer 26:20-23</reference>. Ahikam befriends Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jer 26:24</reference>. <div eID="gen29991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29992" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29993" type="x-p"/> In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim - As this prophecy must have been delivered in the first or second year of the reign of Jehoiakim, it is totally out of its place here. Dr. Blayney puts it before chap. 36.; and Dr. Dahler immediately after chap. ix., and before chap. 46.
entries.cee7c98cd66acc336a91efb59f992f4c91c2d30f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29994" type="x-p"/> If ye will not hearken - This and several of the following verses are nearly the same with those in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.13">Jer 7:13</reference>, etc., where see the notes.
entries.223df8a543f4ee66c44c707e4377df5d6dd38ccc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29995" type="x-p"/> And all the people - That were in company with the priests and the prophets.
entries.d7f1b4c6cadc42bf496ed71a716e3121992c22eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29996" type="x-p"/> The princes of Judah - The king's court; his cabinet counsellors.
entries.e0a1a725a30d2e1ede7dbfe56317a24c108b3804: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29997" type="x-p"/> The Lord sent me to prophesy - My commission is from him, and my words are his own. I sought not this painful office. I did not run before I was sent.
entries.def6710e99f84ac6f2d1694c8e6d54a595a97654: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29998" type="x-p"/> Therefore now amend your ways - If ye wish to escape the judgment which I have predicted, turn to God, and iniquity shall not be your ruin.
entries.3261ebb66bf9f0032005dd3f1c6bc74eefd8c32d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29999" type="x-p"/> As for me, behold, I am in your hand - I am the messenger of God; you may do with me what you please; but if you slay me, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves.
entries.233126fe57e0d344e2d35a30a82a46b9ec2d552a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30000" type="x-p"/> This man is not worthy to die - The whole court acquitted him.
entries.c3fdc8a146a9ab8d3161cc54d0af9470ae7c8e6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30001" type="x-p"/> Certain of the elders - This is really a fine defense, and the argument was perfectly conclusive. Some think that it was Ahikam who undertook the prophet's defense.
entries.9cef2330084bd420779efbbd6c140831355a9f98: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30002" type="x-p"/> Micah the Morasthite - The same as stands among the prophets. Now all these prophesied as hard things against the land as Jeremiah has done; yet they were not put to death, for the people saw that they were sent of God.
entries.e47eb2fd6d118d609c5617e48741c7ff2ff852ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30003" type="x-p"/> Urijah - who prophesied - The process against Jeremiah is finished at the nineteenth verse; and the case of Urijah is next brought on, for he was also to be tried for his life; but hearing of it he fled to Egypt. He was however condemned in his absence; and the king sent to Egypt, and brought him thence and slew him, and caused him to have an ignominious burial, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.21-Jer.26.23">Jer 26:21-23</reference>.
entries.5445af9525c747d08b3bf169627b56e12bb753fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30004" type="x-p"/> The hand of Ahikam - was with Jeremiah - And it was probably by his influence that Jeremiah did not share the same fate with Urijah. The Ahikam mentioned here was probably the father of Gedaliah, who, after the capture of Jerusalem, was appointed governor of the country by Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">Jer 40:5</reference>. Of the Prophet Urijah, whether he was true or false, we know nothing but what we learn from this place. <div eID="gen30004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30005" type="x-p"/> That they should not give him into the hand of the people - Though acquitted in the supreme court, he was not out of danger; there was a popular prejudice against him, and it is likely that Ahikam was obliged to conceal him, that they might not put him to death. The genuine ministers of God have no favor to expect from those who are His enemies.  <chapter eID="Jer.26"/> <div eID="gen30005" type="x-p"/>

entries.3359d6eb33485ce1b4ccb88c9a5c01a4d317fd02: <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1-Jer.26.19">Jer 26:1-19</reference> <div eID="gen14148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14149" type="x-p"/> Accusation and Acquittal of Jeremiah. - <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1">Jer 26:1</reference>-7. His prophecy that temple and city would be destroyed gave occasion to the accusation of the prophet. - Jer 26:1. <hi type="italic">"In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah king of Judah, came this word from Jahveh, saying: </hi> Jer 26:2. <hi type="italic">Thus said Jahveh: Stand in the court of the house of Jahveh, and speak to all the cities of Judah which come to worship in Jahveh’s house, all the words that I have commanded thee to speak to them; take not a word therefrom. </hi> Jer 26:3. <hi type="italic">Perchance they will hearken and turn each from his evil way, that I may repent me of the evil which I purpose to do unto them for the evil of their doings. </hi> Jer 26:4. <hi type="italic">And say unto them: Thus saith Jahveh: If ye hearken not to me, to walk in my law which I have set before you, </hi> Jer 26:5. <hi type="italic">To hearken to the words of my servants the prophets whom I sent unto you, from early morning on sending, but ye have not hearkened. </hi> Jer 26:6. <hi type="italic">Then I make this house like Shiloh, and this city a curse to all the peoples of the earth. </hi> Jer 26:7. <hi type="italic">And the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14150" type="x-p"/> In the discourse of Jer 7, where he was combating the people’s false reliance upon the temple, Jeremiah had already threatened that the temple should share the fate of Shiloh, unless the people turned from its evil ways. Now, since that discourse was also delivered in the temple, and since <reference osisRef="Jer.26.2-Jer.26.6">Jer 26:2-6</reference> of the present chapter manifestly communicate only the substance of what the prophet said, several comm. have held these discourses to be identical, and have taken it for granted that the discourse here referred to, belonging to the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, was given in full in Jer 7, while the history of it has been given in the present chapter by way of supplement (cf. the introductory remarks to Jer 7). But considering that it is a peculiarity of Jeremiah frequently to repeat certain of the main thoughts of his message, the saying of God, that He will do to the temple as He has done to Shiloh, is not sufficient to warrant this assumption. Jeremiah frequently held discourses in the temple, and more than once foretold the destruction of Jerusalem; so that it need not be surprising if on more than one occasion he threatened the temple with the fate of Shiloh. Between the two discourses there is further this distinction: Whereas in Jer 7 the prophet speaks chiefly of the spoliation or destruction of the temple and the expulsion of the people into exile, here in brief incisive words he intimates the destruction of the city of Jerusalem as well; and the present chapter throughout gives the impression that by this, so to speak, peremptory declaration, the prophet sought to move the people finally to decide for Jahveh its God, and that he thus so exasperated the priests and prophets present, that they seized him and pronounced him worthy of death. - According to the heading, this took place in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim. The like specification in the heading of Jer 27 does not warrant us to refer the date to the fourth year of this king. "The beginning" intimates simply that the discourse belongs to the earlier period of Jehoiakim’s reign, without minuter information as to year and day. "To Jeremiah" seems to have been dropped out after "came this word," Jer 26:1. The court of the house of God is not necessarily the inner or priests’ court of the temple; it may have been the outer one where the people assembled; cf. Jer 19:14. All the "cities of Judah" for their inhabitants, as in Jer 11:12. The addition: "take not a word therefrom," cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">Deu 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.13.1">Deu 13:1</reference>, indicates the peremptory character of the discourse. In full, without softening the threat by the omission of anything the Lord commanded him, i.e., he is to proclaim the word of the Lord in its full unconditional severity, to move the people, if possible, to repentance, acc. to Jer 26:3. With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.26.3">Jer 26:3</reference></hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.18.8">Jer 18:8</reference>, etc. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.26.4-Jer.26.6">Jer 26:4-6</reference> we have the contents of the discourse. If they hearken not to the words of the prophet, as has hitherto been the case, the Lord will make the temple as Shiloh, and this city, i.e., Jerusalem, a curse, i.e., an object of curses (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jer 24:9</reference>), for all peoples. On this cf. Jer 7:12. But ye have not hearkened. The <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. הזּאתה Hitz. holds to be an error of transcription; Ew. §173, <hi type="italic">g</hi>, and Olsh. <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §101, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, and 133, a paragogically lengthened form; Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Lehrb</hi>. §665. iii. and 897, 3, a toneless appended suffix, strengthening the demonstrative force: <hi type="italic">this</hi> (city) <hi type="italic">here</hi>.
entries.79b1f8693e033ac779db72bd881eb42eef00bc19: <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20-Jer.26.23">Jer 26:20-23</reference> <hi type="italic">The prophet Urijah put to death.</hi> - While the history we have just been considering gives testimony to the hostility of the priests and false prophets towards the true prophets of the Lord, the story of the prophet Urijah shows the hostility of King Jehoiakim against the proclaimers of divine truth. For this purpose, and not merely to show in how great peril Jeremiah then stood (Gr., Näg.), this history is introduced into our book. It is not stated that the occurrence took place at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, nor can we infer so much from its being placed directly after the events of that time. The time is not specified, because it was irrelevant for the case in hand. Jer 26:20. <hi type="italic">A man, Urijah the son of Shemaiah - both unknown - from Kirjath-Jearim, now called Kuriyet el 'Enab, about three hours to the north-west of Jerusalem, on the frontiers of the tribe of Benjamin </hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>)<hi type="italic">, prophesied in the name of Jahveh against Jerusalem and Judah very much in the same terms as Jeremiah had done. When King Jehoiakim and his great men heard this, discourse, he sought after the prophet to kill him. Urijah, when he heard of it, fled to Egypt; but the king sent men after him, Elnathan the son of Achbor with some followers, and had him brought back thence, caused him to be put to death, and his body to be thrown into the graves of the common people.</hi> Hitz. takes objection to "all his mighty men," <reference osisRef="Jer.26.21">Jer 26:21</reference>, because it is not found in the lxx, and is nowhere else used by Jeremiah. But these facts do not prove that the words are not genuine; the latter of the two, indeed, tells rather in favour of their genuineness, since a glossator would not readily have interpolated an expression foreign to the rest of the book. The "mighty men" are the distinguished soldiers who were about the king, the military commanders, as the "princes" are the supreme civil authorities. <hi type="italic">Elnathan</hi> the son of <hi type="italic">Achbor</hi>, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">Jer 36:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.25">Jer 36:25</reference>, one of Jehoiakim’s princes, was a son of Achbor who is mentioned in 2Ki 22:12-14 as amongst the princes of Josiah. Whether this Elnathan was the same as the Elnathan whose daughter Nehushta was Jehoiachin’s mother (2Ki 24:8), and who was therefore the king’s father-in-law, must remain an undecided point, since the name Elnathan is of not unfrequent occurrence; of Levites, Ezr 8:16. בּני העם (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.17.19">Jer 17:19</reference>) means the common people here, as in 2Ki 22:6. The place of burial for the common people was in the valley of the Kidron; see on 2Ki 22:6.
entries.c09628a15c7bcf3901c89a1380d7681842dc7c69: <reference osisRef="Jer.26.24">Jer 26:24</reference> <div eID="gen14152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14153" type="x-p"/> The narrative closes with a remark as to how, amid such hostility against the prophets of God on the part of king and people, Jeremiah escaped death. This was because the hand of <hi type="italic">Ahikam</hi> the son of <hi type="italic">Shaphan</hi> was with him. This person is named in 2Ki 22:12, 2Ki 22:14, as one of the great men sent by King Josiah to the prophetess Hulda to inquire of her concerning the book of the law recently discovered. According to <reference osisRef="Jer.39.14">Jer 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.5">Jer 40:5</reference>, etc., he was the father of the future Chaldean governor Gedaliah. The Yoke of Babylon upon Judah and the Neighbouring Peoples - Jeremiah 27-29 <div eID="gen14153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14154" type="x-p"/> These three chapters are closely connected with one another. They all belong to the earlier period of Zedekiah’s reign, and contain words of Jeremiah by means of which he confirms and vindicates against the opposition of false prophets his announcement of the seventy years’ duration of the Chaldean supremacy over Judah and the nations, and warns king and people patiently to bear the yoke laid on them by Nebuchadnezzar. The three chapters have besides an external connection. For Jer 28 is attached to the event of Jer 27 by its introductory formula: And it came to pass in <hi type="italic">that</hi> year, at the beginning, etc., as Jer 29 is to Jer 28 by ואלּה. To this, it is true, the heading handed down in the Masoretic text is in contradiction. The date: In the beginning of the reign of <hi type="italic">Jehoiakim</hi>, the son of Josiah king of Judah, came this word to Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">Jer 27:1</reference>), is irreconcilable with the date: And it came to pass in <hi type="italic">that year</hi>, in the beginning of the reign of <hi type="italic">Zedekiah</hi> king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month. The name "Jehoiakim the son of Josiah" in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">Jer 27:1</reference> is erroneous. It is without doubt the blunder of a copyist who had in his mind the heading of the 26th chapter, and should have been "Zedekiah;" for the contents of Jer 27 carry us into Zedekiah’s time, as plainly appears from <reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">Jer 27:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.12">Jer 27:12</reference>, and Jer 27:20. Hence the Syr. translation and one of Kennicott’s codd. have substituted the latter name.<note placement="foot">Following the example of ancient comm., Haevernick in his <hi type="italic">Introd</hi>. (ii. 2) has endeavoured to defend the date: "In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah." To this end he ventures the hypothesis, that in Jer 27 there are placed beside one another three discourses agreeing in their subject-matter: "one addressed to Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.2-Jer.27.11">Jer 27:2-11</reference>), a second to Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12-Jer.27.15">Jer 27:12-15</reference></note>, a third to the priests and people;" and that the words: "by the hand of the ambassador that came to Zedekiah the king of Judah," are appended to show how Zedekiah ought to have obeyed the older prophecy of Jehoiakim’s time, and how he should have borne himself towards the nations with which he was in alliance. but this does not solve the difficulty. The prophecy, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.4-Jer.27.11">Jer 27:4-11</reference>, is addressed to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon; but since the envoys of these kings did not come to Jerusalem till Zedekiah’s time, we are bound, if the prophecy dates from the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, to assume that this prophecy was communicated to Jeremiah and published by him eleven years before the event, upon occasion of which it was to be conveyed to the kings concerned. An assumption that would require unusually cogent reasons to render it credible. Vv. 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi>-21 contain nothing whatever that points to Jehoiakim’s time, or give countenance to the hypothesis that the three sections of this chapter contain three discourses of different dates, which have been put together on account merely of the similarity of their contents. <div eID="gen14154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14155" type="x-p"/> Beyond this one error of transcription, these three chapters contain nothing that could throw any doubt on the integrity of the text. There are no traces of a later supplementary revision by another hand, such as Mov., Hitz., and de W. profess to have discovered. The occurrence of Jeremiah’s name in the contracted form ירמיה, as also of other names compounded with <hi type="italic">Jahu</hi> in the form <hi type="italic">Jah</hi>, does not prove later retouching; for, as Graf has shown, we find alongside of it the fuller form also (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.12">Jer 28:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.27-Jer.29.30">Jer 29:27-30</reference>), and have frequently both longer and shorter forms in the same verse (so in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">Jer 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.12">Jer 28:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.29-Jer.29.31">Jer 29:29-31</reference>). And so long as other means for distinguishing are wanting, it will not do to discriminate the manner of expression in the original text from that of the reviser by means of these forms alone. Again, as we have shown at p. 194, note, there is a good practical reason for Jeremiah’s being called "the prophet" (הנּביא); so that this too is not the reviser’s work. Finally, we cannot argue later addition from the fact that the name of the king of Babylon is written Nebuchad<hi type="italic">n</hi>ezzar in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.6">Jer 27:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">Jer 27:8</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">Jer 27:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.3">Jer 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.11">Jer 28:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.14">Jer 28:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.1">Jer 29:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.3">Jer 29:3</reference>; for the same form appears again in <reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jer 34:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jer 39:5</reference>, and with it we have also Nebuchad<hi type="italic">r</hi>ezzar in <reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">Jer 29:21</reference> and Jer 39:1. Elsewhere, it is true, we find only the one form Nebuchad<hi type="italic">n</hi>ezzar, and this is the unvarying spelling in the books of Kings, Chron., Ezra, Dan., and in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.6">Est 2:6</reference>; whereas Ezekiel uniformly writes Nebuchad<hi type="italic">r</hi>ezzar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7">Eze 26:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18-Ezek.29.19">Eze 29:18-19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.10">Eze 30:10</reference>), and this form Jeremiah uses twenty-seven times (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jer 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.7">Jer 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.25">Jer 22:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1">Jer 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.1">Jer 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jer 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.21">Jer 29:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1">Jer 32:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.28">Jer 32:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">Jer 35:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.1">Jer 37:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jer 39:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11">Jer 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">Jer 43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jer 44:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">Jer 46:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.26">Jer 46:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">Jer 49:28</reference>, 40; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">Jer 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jer 51:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jer 52:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28-Jer.52.30">Jer 52:28-30</reference> - not merely in the discourses, but in the headings and historical parts as well). But though the case is so, we are not entitled to conclude that Nebuchadnezzar was a way of pronouncing the name that came into use at a later time; the conclusion rather is, as we have remarked at p. 203, and on <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan 1:1</reference>, that the writing with <hi type="italic">n</hi> represents the Jewish-Aramaean pronunciation, whereas the form Nebuchadrezzar, according to the testimony of such inscriptions as have been preserved, expresses more fairly Assyrian pronunciation. The Jewish way of pronouncing would naturally not arise till after the king of Babylon had appeared in Palestine, from which time the Jews would have this name often on their lips. Hence it is in the book of Jeremiah alone that we find both forms of the name (that with <hi type="italic">r</hi> 27 times, that with <hi type="italic">n</hi> 10 times). How it has come about that the latter form is used just three times in each of Jer 27 and 28 cannot with certainty be made out. But note, (1) that the form with <hi type="italic">n</hi> occurs twice in 28 (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.3">Jer 28:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.28.11">Jer 28:11</reference>) in the speech of the false prophet Hananiah, and then, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.14">Jer 28:14</reference>, in Jeremiah’s answer to that speech; (2) that the prophecy of Jer 27 was addressed partly to the envoys of the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Phoenicia, while it is partly a warning to the people against the lying speeches of the false prophets, and that it is just in these portions, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.6">Jer 27:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">Jer 27:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">Jer 27:20</reference>, that the name so written occurs. If we consider this, we cannot avoid the conjecture, that by changing the <hi type="italic">r</hi> for <hi type="italic">n</hi>, the Jewish people had accommodated to their own mode of utterance the strange-sounding name <hi type="italic">Nabucudurusur</hi>, and that Jeremiah made use of the popular pronunciation in these two discourses, whereas elsewhere in all his discourses he uses Nebucahd<hi type="italic">r</hi>ezzar alone; for the remaining cases in which we find Nebuchad<hi type="italic">n</hi>ezzar in this book are contained in historical notices.)  <chapter eID="Jer.26"/> <div eID="gen14155" type="x-p"/>

entries.1030bae7275601e7a80dd256c1d09f3be2b1db4e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.26.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.26.1" sID="gen59434" type="section"/> <div sID="gen59435" type="x-p"/>This chapter contains a remarkable history, to which a very useful doctrine is annexed, for Jeremiah speaks of repentance, which forms one of the main points of true religion, and he shews at the same time that the people were rejected by God, because they perversely despised all warnings, and could by no means be brought to a right mind. We shall find these two things in this chapter.<div eID="gen59435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59436" type="x-p"/>He says that this word came to him at the <hi type="italic">beginning of the reign, of Jehoiakim, </hi>of which king we have spoken in other places, where Jeremiah related other discourses delivered in his reign. We hence conclude that this book was not put together in a regular order, but that the chapters were collected, and from them the volume was formed.<div eID="gen59436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59437" type="x-p"/>The time, however, is not here repeated in vain, for we know that the miserable derive some hope from new events. When men have been long afflicted and well-nigh have rotted in their evils, they yet think, when a change takes place, that they shall be happy, and they promise themselves vain hopes. Such was probably the confidence of the people when Jehoiakim began to reign; for they might have thought that things would be restored by him to a better state. There is also another circumstance to be noticed; though their condition was nigh past hope, they yet hardened themselves against God, so that they obstinately resisted the prophets. It hence appears that the reprobate were become more and more exasperated by the scourges of God, and had never been truly and really humbled. This was the reason why Jeremiah, according to God’s command, spoke so sharply.<div eID="gen59437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59438" type="x-p"/>I pass by other things and come to the words, that <hi type="italic">the word of Jehovah came </hi>to him. He thus arrogated nothing to himself; but he testifies how necessary it was, especially among a people so refractory, that he should bring nothing of his own, but announce a truth that came from heaven. A general subject might be here handled, which is, that God alone is to be heard in the Church, and also that no one ought to assume to himself the name of a prophet or teacher, except he whom the Lord has formed and appointed, and to whom he has committed his message; but these things have been treated elsewhere and often and much at large; and I do not willingly dwell long on general subjects. It is then enough to bear in mind the purpose for which Jeremiah says that the word of Jehovah came to him, even that he might secure authority to himself; he does not boast of his own wisdom nor of anything human or earthly, but says only that he spoke what the Lord had commanded him.<div eID="gen59438" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.26.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen59434" osisID="Jer.26.1" type="section"/>
entries.99bdae04149362c16f4952ad07498ab7006ed3e1:
He adds, Thus saith Jehovah, Stand in the court of the house (literally, but house means the Temple) of Jehovah It was not allowed the people to enter into the Temple; hence the Prophet was bidden to abide in the court where he might be heard by all. He was, as we have seen, of the priestly order; but it would have been but of little avail to address the Levites.
Indeed his message does not seem to have been to the priests nor to the false prophets, but to the people who came to worship, as though it was useless to address them.
